etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of あ (a, distal pronominal marker) + の (no, genitive particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From なる (naru, “to become”) + べく (beku, adverbial form of べし (beshi, “possible, able; should”)).
First cited to the 1890s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from 非(ひ)道(どう) (hidō, “evil, inhuman”, adjective ending) + い (-i).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English camp. Doublet of キャンパス (kyanpasu, “campus”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowing from English muffler.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 変(か)える (kaeru), 替(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Abbreviated form of 出入り口.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. 刀 first appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. The furigana カ・タ・ナ for the phonetic attestation of katana only appears centuries later; however, the reading of 刀 in the Nihon Shoki and the Man'yoshu has been generally interpreted as identical to the reconstructed Proto-Japonic *katana.
Commonly suggested as a compound of 片 (kata, “one side”) + な (na, “edge”). This na element is spelled in monolingual Japanese sources as 刃 (“edge, blade”), but there is no historical attestation for any na reading for this character. A comparison with Middle Korean ᄂᆞᆶ〮 (nólh, “blade”) and modern Korean 날 (nal) suggests a Koreanic origin for this latter element. Vovin suggests an Old Korean coordinate term *xʌtʌŋ-nʌrh, due to the nature of the introduction of the specific type of single-edged sabers that are used with katana, mostly introduced from Korea from the 11th century onwards. Compare 直刀 chokutō for a more common reading of 刀 (“sword”) prior to the 11th century.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tau/ → /tɔː/ → /toː/
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 刀 (MC taw). Compare modern Mandarin 刀 (dāo).
First cited as an independent noun to a text from 1895. Cited in compounds since at least the 800s CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yo₂⟩ → */jə/ → /jo/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yə.
In modern Japanese, Japonic よ (yo) is more common than Sinitic し (shi, see Etymology 3) outside fixed compounds, which is similar to 七(なな) (nana) but different from other numerals. The reason may be a superstitious connection to 死(し) (shi, “death”), or simply avoiding confusion with similar sounding 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) and 七(しち) (shichi, “seven”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from yo above, influenced by analogy by the final sound of preceding number 三 (san, “three”). The most common form as a stand-alone number.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/si/ → /ɕi/
From Middle Chinese 四 (MC siɪᴴ).
Compare modern Hakka 四 (si).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Mandarin 四 (sì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 地下(ちか) (chika, “underground”) + 水(すい) (-sui, “water”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 地方 (MC dijH pjang).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 學 (MC haewk, “learning”).
The goon pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 小(こ) (ko-, “little”) + 鳥(とり) (tori, “bird”).
First attested in the late 900s, in the Utsubo Monogatari.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 市(いち) (ichi, “market”) + 場(ば) (ba, “place”). Compare English marketplace.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sinicization of 市場(いちば) (ichiba). See 返事(へんじ) (henji) and 大根(だいこん) (daikon), which have similar etymologies.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from verb 応(おう)ずる (ōzuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) + 拭い (nugui, “wiping; wiper”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 拭(ぬぐ)う (nuguu, “to wipe”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 損 (MC swonX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 最 (sai-, “most”) + 初 (sho, “new, first”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 毛布 (máobù, literally “hair + cloth”), using the expected Japanese readings of the characters. First cited to a text from 1867 with the sense wool fabric.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 満つ (mitu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *mit-.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literally "Seto ware", as Seto City has long been famous for its earthenware.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 物(もの) (mono, “thing”) + 音(おと) (oto, “sound”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 瓶(びん) (bin, “bottle”) + 詰(つ)め (tsume, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 詰(つ)める (tsumeru, “to stuff”).). The tsume changes to zume as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: /syaugai/ → /syoːgai/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The nominalized form of the verb 立てる (tateru, “stand”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle Chinese 程度

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨momi₁ti⟩ → */momʲiti/ → /momʲidi/ → /momid͡ʑi/ → /momiʑi/
Shift from Old Japanese 紅葉 (momi₁ti → momichi).
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical verb 紅葉づ (momizu, “to turn, change color; said of leaves”).
Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 紅葉 /红叶 (hóngyè), see kōyō below.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from Old Japanese 紅葉 (momi₁tiba → momichiba).
Can be parsed as a compound of 紅葉ぢ (momiji, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical verb 紅葉づ (momizu), “to turn in autumn, said of leaves”) + 葉 (ha, “leaf”). The ha changes to ba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kou jepu/ → /koːjefu/ → /koːjeu/ → /koːjoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 紅葉 (MC huwng yep, literally “crimson, red + leaf”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Other various nanori readings.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ti.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 迷惑 (MC mej hwok).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 集む (atumu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 難 (MC nan).
